newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac in call to hustings, stages unity display.
newsitem.headline: Chirac in call to hustings, stages unity display.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac gave his centre-right ministers their election campaign marching orders on Wednesday and staged a show of reconciliation with a former presidential rival, fellow Gaullist Edouard Balladur.

The first opinion poll taken since Chirac dissolved the National Assembly and called a snap election for May 25 and June 1 suggested the ruling coalition would win comfortably but with a sharply reduced majority.
The European Commission meanwhile gave the government a boost by forecasting that France would meet the key criterion for a single European currency this year and next.
Chirac told ministers at a weekly cabinet meeting: "You must continue to govern and fulfil your duties to the full but you are also political leaders.

"You must contribute to feeding the political debate by going out to meet the French people and conveying to them your convictions, your energy, your confidence and your enthusiasm," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted him as saying.
In a pre-election unity gesture, Chirac invited former prime minister Balladur for only their second private meeting since they clashed bitterly for the presidency in 1995.
When Balladur called on Chirac last July, photographers were barred from the Elysee presidential palace courtyard and only managed to shoot grainy pictures through the gates.

The ex-premier, who has stayed away from most coalition and Gaullist party gatherings since Chirac defeated him for the presidency, was given pride of place on the platform on Tuesday when Prime Minister Alain Juppe outlined the government's policy agenda for the election.
Juppe, who on taking office in May 1995 had described the state of the public finances as "calamitous", went out of his way in Wednesday's speech to praise Balladur's record.
Chief Balladur lieutenant Nicolas Sarkozy, also rehabilitated as one of the coalition's spokesmen, ruled out any further austerity measures should the centre-right win.
Asked about opinion poll findings that most French voters expect tougher austerity should the bloc win May-June elections, Sarkozy told RTL radio: "I regret this scepticism.
"There will not be tougher austerity, and no increase in taxes...Of all developed countries, we are the ones with the heaviest burden of taxes," he said.
The opposition Socialists have accused Chirac of preparing a harsh new round of austerity to help meet criteria for joining a planned European single currency.

But the European Commission said on Wednesday that France was on course to meet the toughest test for monetary union by holding its public deficits to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year and next.

Financial markets were calmer after three days of jitters caused by uncertainty generated by the early election. The franc, fixed income and stock markets were stronger partly on the poll showing the centre-right would win.
A CSA institute poll forecast that the centre-right would win 332 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France to 222 for the combined left-wing opposition and one for the extreme-right National Front.
The coalition held 464 of the 577 seats in the outgoing assembly, including most of the 22 seats in French overseas departments and territories which are not covered by opinion polls.
The unpopular Juppe has promised an aggressive campaign to win the poll and lead a modernised France into the European economic and monetary union.

Justice Minister Jacques Toubon renewed Juppe's denial of a report in the investigative weekly Le Canard Enchaine that the Right planned an amnesty for political sleaze if it retained power amid a wave of corruption probes.

"It's pure fabrication, it's slander for electoral purposes just like other themes invented by the Socialists -- "hard capitalism', ultra-liberalism and I don't know what else," Toubon told reporters.
